values.label: Kindness and privacy
values.meaning: Be careful with other people's private stories and help without embarrassing them. If someone is being hurt or feels unsafe, tell a trusted adult.
values.example: A friend spills something: help clean it up without turning their mistake into a joke for everyone.
values.prompt: How can you help someone while protecting their feelings?
values.adultNote: Sutura includes discretion and protecting another person's dignity. This child-facing lesson explicitly protects a child's right to tell a trusted adult about harm; privacy must never become enforced secrecy.

sources.title: Alione Sow: La notion de culture en Wolof (INST)
Niane & Sow: Apport de l'arabe sur les langues nationales du Sénégal (UCAD), pp. 63–64

proverbs.childReading: Respect other people’s privacy. Their personal stories are not always yours to share.
proverbs.connection: The source connects peace with not repeating everything one knows about other people.
proverbs.prompt: Ask before sharing someone else’s personal story. If someone is hurt, scared or unsafe, tell a trusted grown-up.

proverbs.childReading: Kind words can be a gift.
proverbs.connection: The source compares good words to a generous offering; this supports protecting another person’s dignity.
proverbs.prompt: Think of one kind, true thing you can say to someone today.

proverbs.childReading: When you know about a problem, speak up so someone can help.
proverbs.connection: The source says warning someone about a problem is better than knowing and saying nothing. It gives an essential boundary to discretion.
proverbs.prompt: Who is a trusted grown-up you could tell if something worried you?

values.label: Learn good ways
values.meaning: Grow good habits by learning from caring people around you. Practise listening, greeting others, helping, and asking thoughtful questions.
values.example: An older relative shows you how to greet a visitor; you practise, then help a younger child learn too.
values.prompt: What good habit could you learn from someone today?
values.adultNote: Yar concerns upbringing and education in conduct, beyond classroom learning. These activities use guidance and example, with room for questions and boundaries; historical descriptions of punishment are not instructions for children or carers.

sources.title: Boston University: Wolof Proverbs 2 glossary, Yar
Ndoye & Diouf: Integrating traditional values in education (Éthiopiques, excerpted by WATHI)

proverbs.childReading: Good manners help us treat one another with respect.
proverbs.connection: The proverb explicitly uses yaru and the source explains that politeness brings respect.
proverbs.prompt: How could you greet someone, ask for a turn or say thank you?

proverbs.childReading: Asking questions helps us learn.
proverbs.connection: The source directly connects questioning with knowledge.
proverbs.prompt: Ask a grown-up to teach you one Wolof word. Then try using it.

proverbs.childReading: You can always learn something new.
proverbs.connection: The source says it is never too late to study or learn.
proverbs.prompt: What would you like to learn? What is one small way to begin?

values.label: Welcome and share
values.meaning: Help a guest or a newcomer feel welcome and included. Offer your attention, kindness, and what you can share.
values.example: A new child arrives at school: greet them, show them where to sit, and invite them into your game.
values.prompt: What could make someone new feel at home?
values.adultNote: Often translated as hospitality, teraanga also concerns generosity and social relationships. Welcoming others is for everyone; the lesson does not assign hosting to girls or require a child to approach strangers alone.

sources.title: Omar Marone: Teranga Among the Wolof People (Smithsonian, 1990), pp. 48–49
Alione Sow: La notion de culture en Wolof (INST)

proverbs.childReading: Making someone feel welcome matters.
proverbs.connection: The proverb names teraanga and affirms the importance of hospitality.
proverbs.prompt: Someone is new to your group. What could you say to welcome them?

proverbs.childReading: Be ready to give as well as receive.
proverbs.connection: The source asks us not to keep our hands open for receiving but closed for giving.
proverbs.prompt: What could you share today: a pencil, your time or a turn?

proverbs.childReading: Make room for everyone in the conversation.
proverbs.connection: The source compares conversation to a shared meal and says everyone present has a right to take part.
proverbs.prompt: At your next group conversation, invite someone who has not had a turn to speak.

values.label: Respect yourself
values.meaning: Value yourself and take care with what you do. Try your best, admit mistakes, and make things right.
values.example: You knock over a friend's work: say what happened and help rebuild it, even when admitting it feels hard.
values.prompt: What is something you can do today that you will feel proud of?
values.adultNote: Jom can encompass self-respect, honour, resolve, and responsibility. This lesson is for every child; worth does not depend on winning, gender, wealth, or hiding a need for help.

sources.title: Boston University: Wolof Proverbs 7 glossary, Jom
Niane & Sow: Apport de l'arabe sur les langues nationales du Sénégal (UCAD), pp. 63–64

proverbs.childReading: Keep trying when a good task becomes difficult.
proverbs.connection: The source explicitly urges perseverance instead of abandoning a project because of difficulties.
proverbs.prompt: Name a task that feels hard. What is one small next step? You can ask for help.

proverbs.childReading: Show what you can do by taking a step and trying.
proverbs.connection: The proverb contrasts saying “I can do it” with actually doing it.
proverbs.prompt: Choose one helpful thing you can do today, then have a go.

proverbs.childReading: Be honest and take care of what is trusted to you, even when no one is watching.
proverbs.connection: The source explicitly connects honesty without supervision with caring for what has been entrusted to us.
proverbs.prompt: You find a pencil that is not yours. How can you help it get back to its owner?

values.label: Thoughtful words and actions
values.meaning: Pause and choose words and actions that show consideration for others. Give people room to speak, and share your own ideas respectfully.
values.example: You disagree during a game: wait for your friend to finish, then explain your idea without insulting them.
values.prompt: How can you disagree while still showing respect?
values.adultNote: Kersa carries meanings of modesty, restraint, and regard for others. This adaptation teaches consideration without making silence, embarrassment, or obedience the measure of a child's goodness.

sources.title: Alione Sow: La notion de culture en Wolof (INST)
Niane & Sow: Apport de l'arabe sur les langues nationales du Sénégal (UCAD), pp. 63–64

proverbs.childReading: Listen and understand before you answer.
proverbs.connection: The source directly asks the listener to understand before replying.
proverbs.prompt: Let someone finish speaking. Can you say what you heard before you reply?

proverbs.childReading: There is room for another person’s voice.
proverbs.connection: The source uses room for salt in a cooking pot to explain that everyone present may participate in a conversation.
proverbs.prompt: How could you make room for a quiet friend’s idea?

proverbs.childReading: Pause and think before you speak.
proverbs.connection: The source warns that speaking without thinking leads to mistakes.
proverbs.prompt: Before you speak, ask yourself: is it true, and can I say it kindly?

values.label: Patience and effort
values.meaning: The things we learn can take time. Take a breath, keep practising, and ask for help when you need it.
values.example: A knot will not come undone: slow down, try another way, or ask someone to show you.
values.prompt: What helps you keep going when learning feels difficult?
values.adultNote: Muñ means to be patient, persevere, or endure. Patience can include resting and getting help; children need not tolerate pain or mistreatment.

sources.title: Boston University: Wolof Proverbs 6 glossary, Muñ
Boston University: Wolof Proverbs 3 glossary, Muñ

proverbs.childReading: Be patient: something good may come with time.
proverbs.connection: The source directly connects patience with smiling. “May” avoids promising that every wait ends well.
proverbs.prompt: What helps you wait for your turn without rushing someone else?

proverbs.childReading: Some things take time. Give them a chance.
proverbs.connection: The image of waiting at a well for a bucket illustrates patience.
proverbs.prompt: Think of a seed growing. What can you do while you wait?

proverbs.childReading: Small steps can help us do big things.
proverbs.connection: The source explicitly explains that big tasks can be achieved through little steps.
proverbs.prompt: Break a big job into three small steps. Which one can you do first?

values.label: Loyalty and trust
values.meaning: Build trust by caring for your friendships and keeping the promises you can keep. Remember and appreciate the people who help you.
values.example: A friend lends you a book: take care of it, return it when you agreed, and thank them.
values.prompt: What small promise could you make and keep?
values.adultNote: The term includes gratitude, loyalty, and trust in relationships. Loyalty allows honest disagreement and asking for help; no promise requires a child to conceal harm.

sources.title: Boston University: Wolof Proverbs 6 glossary, Kóllëré

proverbs.childReading: Care for what someone has trusted you with, even when they are not there.
proverbs.connection: The source links honesty with managing well what has been entrusted to us; this supports reliability in relationships.
proverbs.prompt: If you borrow a toy, how can you take care of it and return it?

proverbs.childReading: Remember to thank the people who helped you.
proverbs.connection: The source explains that when we enjoy something, we should thank the person who made it possible.
proverbs.prompt: Who helped you today? Tell them what you appreciated.

proverbs.childReading: Let honesty guide you.
proverbs.connection: The source names honesty as a person’s best protection; this supports trustworthy relationships.
proverbs.prompt: If you make a mistake, how could you tell the truth and help put it right?

values.label: Make peace
values.meaning: Help people live and play peacefully together. Listen during disagreements and look for a fair way forward.
values.example: Two children want the same toy: ask what each needs and help them agree on taking turns.
values.prompt: What could help everyone feel heard in a disagreement?
values.adultNote: Jàmm means peace and appears in everyday greetings. Peace includes safety and fairness; children can seek adult help with bullying or conflict.

sources.title: Boston University: Wolof Proverbs 7 glossary, Jàmm

proverbs.childReading: Peace makes room for everyone.
proverbs.connection: The source describes peace as a place where all people can be at ease.
proverbs.prompt: What could make your classroom or home feel peaceful for everyone?

proverbs.childReading: We can do more when we work together.
proverbs.connection: The source uses one hand being unable to clap to explain cooperation toward a shared goal.
proverbs.prompt: Choose a small job to do together. How will you share the work?

proverbs.childReading: Talking and listening can help clear up a misunderstanding.
proverbs.connection: The source connects misunderstanding with a lack of discussion. The child version avoids claiming conversation solves every conflict.
proverbs.prompt: If two friends disagree, what could each say to explain what happened?
